title: A Protocol for Bioinspired Design: A Ground Sampler Based on Sea Urchin Jaws
protocol: Wear personal protective equipment.
Rinse forceps and scalpel with distilled water.
Thaw a frozen pink sea urchin at room temperature for 1 hour.
Place the thawed specimen in a glass dish with sufficient space.
Turn the urchin upside down so that the teeth tips face up.
Cut away the connective tissue around the perimeter of Aristotle's lantern with the scalpel.
Carefully lift out the lantern and rinse it off with running distilled water.
Discard unused urchin parts in a proper waste disposal container.
Turn the Aristotle's lantern over again to have the tips of the teeth facing down.
Locate the plumula end of each tooth facing up.
Use forceps to carefully slide out individual teeth from the lantern.
Weigh 5 g of resin and add 1.15 g of hardener in a shallow disposable plastic tray.
Mix contents together slowly without forming bubbles.
Keep any leftover mixed epoxy in a well-ventilated fume hood away from flammable items.
Lubricate a 2.5 dram plastic tube using petroleum jelly applied with a finger.
Wipe off excess petroleum jelly with a tissue.
Fill the tube halfway with mixed epoxy.
Use forceps to pick up a tooth and carefully submerge it in the epoxy with the curved concave side facing up.
Let the epoxy cure at room temperature for 24 hours.
Place the plastic tube with cured epoxy in a vise.
Tighten the vise slowly until a fissure is made in the plastic tube.
Peel away residual plastic from the epoxy surface.
Cut the epoxy around the tooth down to a smaller block (1 cm³) using a sectioning saw.
Prepare a clean area for polishing and set up a flat work station with a hard plastic board.
Fill a squirt bottle with distilled water.
Start with the lowest grit sandpaper available.
Squeeze a small amount of water from the wash bottle onto the sandpaper.
Using light pressure, rub the sample in one back and forth direction (e.g., left-right) for 5 minutes.
Wash off the surface of the sample over a sink.
Wipe off the sample with a particle-free tissue.
Remove any leftover sandpaper grit with compressed air for 15 seconds.
Use progressively higher grit sandpaper (e.g., 600 and 2,400) to repeat protocol steps 1.6.1 and 1.6.2.
Rub the sample in a back and forth direction perpendicular to the previous polish step using light pressure.
Prepare a squirt bottle with 3-µm diamond polishing suspension in a 1:1 distilled water solution.
Use a polish cloth for diamond suspensions to repeat protocol steps 1.6.1 and 1.6.2.
Prepare a squirt bottle with 0.5-µm alumina polishing suspension in a 1:1 distilled water solution.
Use a microcloth polishing surface to repeat protocol steps 1.6.1 and 1.6.2.
Polish for 5 min in a back and forth motion to remove all previous scratches.
Clean the polished surface with distilled water.
Dry the polished surface carefully using particle-free tissue with compressed air.
Wrap the polished surface with particle-free tissue to maintain a mirror-polished finish.
Dry all polishing surfaces face down on large particle-free tissues.
Characterize the sea urchin tooth microstructure using scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
Sputter iridium onto the polished tooth surface with a deposition current of 85 mA for 10 seconds to achieve a coating thickness of ~20 nm.
Obtain micrograph images at magnifications ranging from 250X to 4,000X using SEM.
Use 5 kV in scanning electron (SE) mode and 15 kV in back-scattered electron (BSE) mode for imaging.
Utilize BSE mode to identify calcite fibers interspersed with Mg-enriched polycrystalline matrix.
Perform micro-computed tomography (µ-CT) scans of a whole pink sea urchin and a freshly dissected Aristotle's lantern.
Position each thawed sample inside the closed chamber container with a moistened tissue to maintain humidity during scanning.
Scan the whole urchin at an isotropic voxel size of 36.00 µm using an electrical potential of 100 kVp and current of 100 mA, applying a 1.0 mm aluminum filter.
Scan the Aristotle's lantern at an isotropic voxel size of 9.06 µm with an electrical potential of 70 kVp and current of 141 mA, using a 1.0 mm aluminum filter.
Apply beam hardening correction algorithm during image reconstruction to correct for beam hardening artifacts from the µ-CT x-ray source.
Refine image segmentation and acquire a triangle mesh model for the Aristotle's lantern structure using imaging software.
Load Aristotle's lantern image data from the µ-CT scan.
Match the voxel size to 9.06 µm.
Use a volume rendering function to visualize the Aristotle's lantern in 3D space.
Adjust the 2D orthogonal slice with the Bounding Box module.
Adjust the threshold value/color with the Volume Rendering module.
Make mask segments for the region of interest using the segmentation editor.
Select XY, YZ, and XZ planes.
Select the 3D isometric view.
Use the magic wand to distinguish between simple structures in the Aristotle's lantern.
Reconstruct the model surface from the extracted mask segments.
Select the Surface Generation module and apply.
Deselect the Volume Rendering Settings to have the visible top surface disappear.
Add the Surface View module to display the surface result.
Simplify the model surface by reducing the number of faces to < 18,000.
Edit individual triangle mesh on the model surface as needed.
Save the model as a stereolithography (STL) file for exporting.
Save the STL file parts to a flash drive and upload them to an FDM 3D printer.
Load acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) plastic cartridges into the appropriate slots of the 3D printer.
Load support plastic material cartridges into the designated slots of the 3D printer.
Insert the modeling base on the Z platform, aligning tabs with slots on the metal tray.
Open each STL file part and follow the display screen steps to print all lantern parts simultaneously.
Arrange all five teeth on the modeling base for printing with the tooth tip facing up.
Release the modeling base from the tabs when all file parts are printed.
Slide the base out of the 3D printer along the tray guides.
Use a metal spatula to pry all parts off the base.
Use a metal file to wear down any extra plastic attached to the parts.
Place the printed parts into a heated base bath until support material dissolves.
Fasten each tooth to a joint arm with a link rod and two E-retaining rings on either side.
Open the file (xx.sldprt) in SolidWorks Simulation.
Select the "Study Advisor" button and then choose "New Study".
Choose the type of simulation test as "Static".
Right-click on "Fixtures" and select "Fixed Geometry".
Add fixtures to the inner faces where pins will go.
Right-click on "External Loads" and select "Force".
Apply 45 N force to the tooth grinding tip faces.
Right-click on "External Loads" and select "Gravity".
Indicate "Top Plane" for the gravity force applied normal to the plane.
On the Static Test list, right-click on "Mesh" and select "Create Mesh".
Move the scale bar for "Mesh Density" all the way to the right for "Fine".
Right-click on "Static" and select "Run" to run the test.
